title: Before the sun goes down (Ephesians 4:25–32)
hookLine: be angry but don't sin; be kind, tender-hearted, forgiving
tomorrow: why would a man in chains write about armor?

lines: BE YE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.
cards: The fight happened at four. It's nine now, and you're still replaying it in the shower, winning this time. Paul has a line for exactly this, and it surprises people: "Be ye angry, and sin not."
Not a ban on anger. He seems to expect it. What he cares about is how long it stays, and he sets the deadline in the very next words: "let not the sun go down upon your wrath."
Sunset. Anger can come in the door. It isn't allowed to move in and unpack.

teach.b: Here's one to tell a friend: be ye angry, and sin not wasn't new with Paul. His words echo a line from Psalm four, as it reads in the old Greek translation of the Psalms. Why the deadline?
Give place: hand over a room. Anger kept overnight, then a week, then years, becomes a room something else can live in.

teach.h: STOP ONE THING, START ITS OPPOSITE.
teach.b: Then Paul gives a run of commands, and each has the same shape: stop one thing, start its opposite. Lying gives way to truth, "for we are members one of another."

Stealing gives way to giving: "let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth." Harsh talk gives way to words that "minister grace unto the hearers."
Then the list to clear out: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you." And what moves into the empty room?
"And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you." Paul doesn't say forgive because they've earned it.
He says forgive as you've been forgiven.
One honest note: settling anger isn't the same as rushing back to someone who hurts you. Sometimes the step before sunset happens inside you.

how: Some Christian couples and families take Ephesians 4:26 as a rule not to let a quarrel run overnight, and Ephesians 4:32 is read in some churches at weddings and services of reconciliation.

games.q: what does “before the sun goes down” mean?
o: an evening prayer said at sunset
a curfew for children before dark
settling anger the same day it starts

games.q: stop one thing, start another — tap the pairs.
p: even as God… hath forgiven you

s: the Bible says all anger is a sin
a popular belief. be ye angry, and sin not: Paul expects anger and limits how long it stays.
Paul says forgive people because they deserve it
even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you: forgiven people forgive.
Paul's cure for stealing is working so you can give
that he may have to give to him that needeth.

games.q: a coworker admits he's been taking supplies home from the office and wants to stop for good. what's Paul's replacement?
o: work with his hands at something good, so he has something to give.
just stop; nothing needs to take the habit's place.
confess in front of everyone and pay a fine.
games.why: let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour… that he may have to give to him that needeth. every command in the passage swaps a harm for its opposite.

practice: Name one anger you're carrying today, in a single sentence. Name what keeps you holding it: pride, fear, or just being right.
Then choose one step before sunset, a short apology, a kind word, or, where talking isn't safe, a quiet decision to stop replaying it.

wordCard.voice: Before the sun goes down. Paul's deadline on anger: feel it, don't sin in it, and don't let it stay the night.

orig.note: Greek: anger, wrath. One of the words in Paul's list to put away, Ephesians 4:31.

carryVoice: Your line: kind, tenderhearted, forgiving, as you've been forgiven. The sun's still up. See you tomorrow.
